thesis: The strongest search hypothesis is inexpensive, genuinely additional access to an effective service—not housing, or any organization category, in the abstract.
assumptionBoundary: The registry contains heterogeneous exploratory models, not 25 independent measurements or current marginal funding offers. A central scenario is not an expected value over quantified probabilities.

researchPriorities.title: Remove a small barrier to a large health benefit
researchPriorities.claim: Test whether navigation, supplies or timely access unlock care that already has clinical and public infrastructure.
researchPriorities.support: Medication access, earlier clinical care, glasses and naloxone illustrate the mechanism. Cheap donor cash may rely on substantial publicly funded or donated resources.
researchPriorities.falsifier: Existing services would reach the same people anyway, the missing resource is not money, or completed effective treatment does not increase.

researchPriorities.title: Target severe, avoidable harm rather than broad reach
researchPriorities.claim: A low-cost intervention has more scope when untreated risk or impairment is high.
researchPriorities.support: Fatal-risk and vision models are highly sensitive to recipient selection. Contacts and city-average risk do not identify the relevant subgroup.
researchPriorities.falsifier: The reachable marginal recipients have mild impairment, low untreated risk or good alternative coverage.

researchPriorities.title: Buy durable benefit without buying an expensive full bundle
researchPriorities.claim: Compare a marginal access increment with its own counterfactual, not an entire system's average budget.
researchPriorities.support: Short housing acceleration and crisis diversion yield only days or weeks of modeled health; lifetime mortality and credential models depend heavily on persistence assumptions.
researchPriorities.falsifier: Benefits fade quickly, completion is poor, recurrent events duplicate lifetime credit or the proposed cheap increment cannot operate independently.

researchPriorities.title: Treat housing as several mechanisms, not one finding
researchPriorities.claim: Preventing a cash shortfall, averting legal displacement, providing a long subsidy and readying a vacant room are different interventions.
researchPriorities.support: GLIDE, Compass and Hamilton share a VA simulation transfer. EDC, Larkin and THC use different health-time judgments and causal endpoints.
researchPriorities.falsifier: Comparable costs and health-state assumptions erase the apparent gap; a housing outcome does not improve health relative to the actual alternative.

researchPriorities.title: Investigate policy leverage, but earn every attribution link
researchPriorities.claim: A small policy grant could affect many people; large scale is a hypothesis to test after the two candidate cohorts.
researchPriorities.support: The policy phase will separately assess SPUR, GrowSF and HAC. No policy or election win is treated as a QALY.
researchPriorities.falsifier: The change would happen anyway, is not implemented, displaces another improvement or does not change health-relevant outcomes.

costLedger.name: Marginal donor cash
costLedger.question: What extra delivery does this dated gift buy after replacement financing?
costLedger.boundary: Do not infer it from a public contract ceiling, donation button or historical average.

costLedger.name: Total incremental resources
costLedger.question: What clinical care, public reimbursement, volunteer time, donated goods and infrastructure are also required?
costLedger.boundary: Low private cash cost does not make those resources free; record whether they can expand.

costLedger.name: Net payer or societal cost
costLedger.question: Which downstream costs change causally, and who captures the saving?
costLedger.boundary: Hospital savings are not automatically money returned to the donor or additional QALYs.

causalLedger: Specify the recipient subgroup, program dose and realistic alternative.
Price incremental delivery and all complementary resources.
Estimate additional completed outcomes, excluding funding replacement and alternative access.
Translate those outcomes into person-level health utility or survival over an explicit horizon.
Account for overlap, repeated events, null/harm, and shared evidence before comparing or aggregating.
nextOrder: SPUR, GrowSF and Housing Action Coalition
Final strongest-four selection and GiveWell-style visual rebuild
